name: Cryptic crossword No 26,666
preamble: Five of the thematic solutions have something in common, not further defined in their clues

clue.text: Home adopted by the Guardian

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in and keep, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: a newspaper speaks of itself in editorials as 'we'
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A house or a cause has been taken up by the Guardian newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: This is one of the five thematic answers the preamble leaves undefined: things the Romans gave us in the Monty Python sketch. The setter's own paper speaks as 'we'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the famous Life of Brian scene, wine is listed among the benefits brought by Roman occupation.

clue.text: Excuse me? Did some old people at any time cause our ruin? That's a funny revolutionary line

annotation.answer: WHAT HAVE THE ROMANS EVER DONE FOR US

blocks.note: a blunt way of asking someone to repeat themselves
the past question 'did ... ?' recast in the perfect tense
an ancient people
at any time
to be done for is to be ruined

explanation.surface: A puzzled questioner wonders whether some ancient race brought about our downfall, then praises it as a good revolutionary joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay paraphrases the question piece by piece in clue order. The revolutionaries are the People's Front of Judea in Monty Python's film Life of Brian.
explanation.definitionFit: The question is the famous comic speech by a rebel leader in Monty Python's Life of Brian, a film about anti-Roman insurgents in Judea.

clue.text: Feel shame, seeing horse in pen

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: to pen is to write
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Someone is embarrassed to find a horse shut in a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: The pen looks like a farmyard enclosure but is the verb to write; horse is drug slang for heroin, whose symbol is H.
explanation.definitionFit: To writhe is to squirm, as one does with acute embarrassment or mortification.

clue.text: Obliged to look over opponents

indicators.note: in a down entry, being over something means placed above it, so the first piece comes before the second

blocks.note: behold is an old word for look
East and North are opposing partnerships at the bridge table

explanation.surface: Someone is duty-bound to keep an eye on their rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, players sit as North, South, East and West, with East and North on opposite sides, a common crossword source for pairs of compass letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being beholden means owing a debt of gratitude or duty to someone, which is being indebted.

clue.text: A short clever answer is capital

indicators.note: something cut short loses its tail end

blocks.note: taken as written
SMART, clever, without its final letter
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A brief witty reply is judged first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as an exclamation of approval, but it is the noun: a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmara is the capital city of Eritrea, in the Horn of Africa.

clue.text: Bog briefly venerated by 10

definitions.note: the definition means 'a god worshipped by the Romans', 10 being THE ROMANS

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is clipped of its final letter

blocks.note: MARSH, a bog, with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: A swamp briefly became an object of Roman worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 points to part of the long linked answer, THE ROMANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars was the Roman god of war, worshipped widely and honoured in the month March.

clue.text: 12 across in curried food business

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: curried food is hot and spicy
12 across is PEACE, and 'Sh!' is a call for peace and quiet

explanation.surface: A note on something tucked inside a curry house's trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference must be solved first and then turned into a synonym: 'Peace!' and 'Sh!' are both demands for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishery is a place or enterprise where fish are caught or farmed for sale as food.

clue.text: Lionel, a hot favourite at Christmas?

blocks.note: Lionel Messi, the Argentine footballer
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A star footballer is hotly tipped as the festive season's top pick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot favourite' looks like betting talk, but 'hot' is just H. The question mark flags a definition by example: a seasonal concert staple. Brian is famously mistaken for the Messiah in the film.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel's oratorio Messiah is performed by choirs everywhere at Christmas, so it is a perennial seasonal favourite.

clue.text: Deal here in broken toys

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper is told to trade in damaged toys here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' looks like a verb, but it is a town, capitalised by its position at the start of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Deal is a seaside town on the east coast of the English county of Kent, so Kent is where it lies.

clue.text: See 2
Drink while young — make mine purer when brewed

definitions.note: describes wine sold young rather than naming a drink

indicators.note: brewing mixes and transforms its ingredients, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to drink something early, and to make your own brew cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the surface read as two instructions; the second is the wordplay, with 'make' only linking.
explanation.definitionFit: En primeur is French wine-trade jargon for wine bought young, before bottling, when the vintage is new.

clue.text: An expert in the gymnasium?

blocks.note: PE, physical education, is what happens in the school gym
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: Someone asks who the champion is down at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the five thematic answers, given no definition: in the sketch, the Romans are credited with bringing peace. An ace at PE is the expert in the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pax Romana, the long calm under the empire, is the last benefit grudgingly listed in the Life of Brian scene.

clue.text: Sit, keeping one's balance

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A command to sit while staying steady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' reads as a possessive, but it is 'one is': the I is held, and 'is' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Poise is graceful steadiness and composure, the state of being well balanced.

clue.text: It helps feet go on platforms

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: podia is the plural of podium, a raised platform
a go is an attempt, a try

explanation.surface: Platform shoes, it seems, are good for the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on platforms' sounds like boarding a train or wearing tall shoes; 'go' is the noun, an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Podiatry is chiropody, the medical care and treatment of disorders of the foot.

clue.text: A part of Norfolk that's not British

indicators.note: something that is not there has been taken away

blocks.note: the Broads are the lakes and rivers of the Norfolk wetlands
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A region of an English county is said to be un-British.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the five thematic answers, given no definition. The Norfolk Broads are a network of navigable lakes and rivers in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman roads are among the benefits reluctantly listed by the rebels in the famous Life of Brian scene.

clue.text: Two elements essential to our existence (and to 16 across?)

definitions.note: a hint rather than a synonym: the word that leads into 16 across in the film title

blocks.note: first element: Li, the symbol for lithium
second element: Fe, the symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A pair of chemical elements is vital to us, and to someone else too.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket points to 16 across: the film is Life of Brian. 'Essential to' looks like part of the wordplay but only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Life is the state of being alive, the whole of a person's being in the world.

clue.text: Queen may, we hear, be confused with 8

definitions.note: means 'the one confused with 8', a name rather than a verb

blocks.note: first meaning: Queen's May, as heard aloud, is the rock band's guitarist with this first name
second meaning: the hero of the Monty Python film, mistaken for the Messiah

explanation.surface: A monarch might be mixed up with a holy figure, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' is not the monarch but the band; 'Queen may' heard as 'Queen's May' points to its guitarist Brian May. 8 is MESSIAH.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian May plays guitar in Queen, and Brian Cohen is the reluctant hero taken for a saviour in Life of Brian.

clue.text: Firm moves into sort of market with no room left

indicators.note: things that move change position, so these letters are rearranged
going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: a bull market is one where prices are rising
taken as written

explanation.surface: A company enters a crowded market where there's no space left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like the company doing the moving; its letters are the ones that move.
explanation.definitionFit: Brim-full means filled right up to the brim, so completely full that nothing more fits.

clue.text: A girl, not a son?  I'm not happy about that

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to leave something out

blocks.note: taken as written
LASS, a girl, without one S
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent laments that the new baby is a daughter rather than a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the standard abbreviation for son, as in genealogies; it comes off the girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of sorrow or regret, expressing unhappiness at some piece of news.

clue.text: A line abandoned by Europe, avoided in hearing

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so letters drop out
something in hearing is judged by how it sounds rather than its spelling

blocks.note: taken as written
a line of people waiting is a queue
EU, the European Union
to duck something is to avoid it

explanation.surface: A railway line was dropped by Europe and dodged in a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the five thematic answers, given no definition. QUEUE loses EU, leaving QUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The aqueduct is the first Roman achievement cited in the Life of Brian scene, carrying water to cities.

clue.text: Brief order to stop working

indicators.note: made brief, a word is clipped of its end
to stop a hole is to plug it, so one piece fills the middle of another

blocks.note: a working is an excavation such as a mine
EDICT, an order, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A curt instruction to down tools.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the five thematic answers, given no definition. 'Working' looks like an adjective, but it is the noun: a mine or quarry is a working.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicine is among the benefits of Roman rule grudgingly admitted in the Life of Brian scene.

clue.text: To remove electrons from position is easy

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the words that follow

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A physics note: stripping electrons off is easy from a certain position.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a chemistry claim; the answer straddles the three final words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionising an atom means converting it to a charged ion, often by stripping away one or more electrons.

clue.text: Savages bad housing that holds area back

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it inside
going back means running the other way

blocks.note: a slum is squalid housing
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Wild people rough up some slum housing that restrains part of a region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savages' looks like a plural noun, but it is the verb: attacks fiercely.
explanation.definitionFit: To maul is to attack and tear with claws or teeth, the way an animal savages its prey.

clue.text: What hurts me in Indian city

blocks.note: the possessive form for me
a sore is a painful spot

explanation.surface: A traveller asks what is causing them pain somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What hurts me' is read as 'my sore': the pain that belongs to me.
explanation.definitionFit: Mysore, now officially Mysuru, is a large historic city in the southern Indian state of Karnataka.

clue.text: See 2
Patsy's English, looked down on by Irish party

indicators.note: in a down entry, what is looked down on lies below, so it comes second

blocks.note: the DUP, the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Patsy is English, and the Irish crowd look down on her for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Patsy looks like a woman's name, but it is the American word for a victim or fall guy; the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A patsy is someone easily cheated or set up to take the blame, which is a dupe or gull.

clue.text: Expected learner to get to the end of Pushkin

blocks.note: something due is expected
L for learner, as on a British learner driver's L-plate

explanation.surface: A student is supposed to reach the last page of a Russian classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of Pushkin' looks like an instruction to take his last letter, N; it is his death.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet Alexander Pushkin died of wounds received in a pistol duel in 1837, so a duel ended him.

clue.text: See 2
Paul had one for 10

blocks.note: surface reading: someone called Paul has a thing set aside for ten people
setter's reading: 10 is THE ROMANS, and St Paul wrote a New Testament letter addressed to them

explanation.walkthrough: 10 points to THE ROMANS from the long linked answer; Paul is the apostle, whose Letter to the Romans is a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal letter, and the New Testament letters of the apostles are called the Epistles.

clue.text: B___ awful noise made by group together

blocks.note: the letter B, dressed up as a censored swear word
a racket is a loud unpleasant din

explanation.surface: A band playing together makes a bloody awful noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The blanked word reads as an expletive like 'bloody', but only its first letter, B, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To bracket things is to class or link them as belonging in the same category or set.
